title: Calculus II
description: Calculus II extends the first course from basic accumulation to a flexible theory and practice of integration, infinite processes, approximation, and dynamic models. Everyone studies the same mathematical core, while problem sets and labs rotate through life-science, engineering, computing, economic, chemical, and mathematical contexts. The course emphasizes exact, numerical, graphical, proof-aware, and model-based reasoning.

topics.title: Integral Foundations and Strategy
topics.description: Calculus II begins by consolidating the definite integral, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and substitution. The deeper goal is to diagnose an integrand, choose a defensible method, and verify the result rather than memorize disconnected tricks.

children.title: Fundamental Theorem and net change review
children.description: The Fundamental Theorem remains the conceptual anchor: integrals accumulate and antiderivatives evaluate that accumulation.

children.title: Accumulation functions and both parts of the Fundamental Theorem
Net change, signed accumulation, and total accumulation
Average value and units of a definite integral
Substitution and inverse chain-rule structure
children.description: Substitution succeeds when the integrand contains a composite function together with the differential pattern of its inner function.

children.title: Algebraic, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic patterns
Integration strategy
children.description: A good integrator first simplifies and classifies the expression, then selects the least complicated method that matches its structure.

children.title: Algebraic division, factoring, identities, and completing the square
Recognizing substitution, parts, trigonometric, and rational-function structures
Combining methods in a planned sequence
Explaining why a chosen method fits and why alternatives do not

topics.title: Integration by Parts and Reduction Ideas
topics.description: Integration by parts reverses the product rule. It is essential for products, logarithms, inverse trigonometric functions, and recurring integral families, and it introduces the idea of transforming a problem into a simpler one.

children.title: Deriving and applying integration by parts
children.description: The formula is most useful when one factor becomes simpler when differentiated and the other remains integrable.

children.title: Choosing u and dv using structural judgment rather than a rigid mnemonic
Repeated integration by parts and tabular organization
Products and special functions
children.description: Many common antiderivatives become accessible only after treating one factor as an implicit product with 1.

children.title: Polynomial times exponential or trigonometric functions
Reduction and recursive relationships
children.description: A reduction formula expresses a difficult integral in terms of a related, simpler case and reveals patterns useful in computation and analysis.

children.title: Optional computational implementation of a reduction rule

topics.title: Trigonometric Integrals and Trigonometric Substitution
topics.description: Trigonometric identities and substitutions turn powers and radical expressions into integrable forms. The point is not identity collection; it is matching algebraic geometry to a useful parameterization.

children.title: Powers and products of sine and cosine
children.description: Parity determines which identity or factorization exposes a substitution.

children.title: Odd powers and saving one factor
Powers of tangent and secant
children.description: Tangent-secant integrals use derivative pairings and Pythagorean identities that differ from sine-cosine cases.

children.title: Even secant powers and reserving secant-squared
Odd tangent powers and reserving secant-tangent
Trigonometric substitution for radicals
children.description: A substitution based on a right-triangle identity removes square roots associated with circles and hyperbolas.

children.title: Patterns involving a^2-x^2, a^2+x^2, and x^2-a^2
Choosing sine, tangent, or secant substitutions

topics.title: Rational Functions and Partial Fractions
topics.description: Partial fractions decomposes a complicated rational function into standard pieces. It is a systematic algebraic algorithm with applications in differential equations, systems, transforms, and economic dynamics.

children.title: Preparation and decomposition
children.description: The method applies to proper rational functions after division and factorization of the denominator.

children.title: Polynomial long division for improper rational functions
Irreducible quadratic factors and repeated quadratics
Finding coefficients
children.description: Coefficients can be found by equating polynomials, strategic substitution, or efficient cover-up in appropriate linear cases.

children.title: Systems of equations for repeated or quadratic factors
Recombining fractions to verify the decomposition
Integrating decomposed terms
children.description: Each component maps to a small library of logarithmic, power, or arctangent antiderivatives.

children.title: Completing the square for quadratic terms
Combining partial fractions with substitution or other methods

topics.title: Numerical Integration and Approximation Error
topics.description: Exact antiderivatives may be unavailable or unnecessary when data are sampled. Numerical integration converts finite function values into reliable approximations and makes error a first-class part of the answer.

children.title: Quadrature rules
children.description: Each rule replaces the function by a simpler local approximation and integrates that approximation exactly.

children.title: Simpson's rule and its polynomial intuition
Error bounds and refinement
children.description: A numerical result must be paired with evidence about its accuracy and sensitivity to step size.

children.title: Qualitative error from monotonicity and concavity
Computational implementation
children.description: A short spreadsheet or program makes the algorithm transparent and prepares students for later numerical methods.

children.title: Constructing nodes, widths, weights, and sampled values
Comparing methods on a function with a known integral
Documenting inputs, assumptions, precision, and stopping decisions

topics.title: Improper Integrals and Continuous Tails
topics.description: Improper integrals extend accumulation to infinite intervals and unbounded integrands. Their value is defined through limits, so convergence must be established before algebraic evaluation is trusted.

children.title: Infinite intervals
children.description: An integral over an unbounded interval is a limit of integrals over finite intervals.

children.title: Splitting at a finite point when both tails are infinite
Interpreting finite total mass, probability, or exposure over an infinite horizon
Unbounded integrands
children.description: A vertical asymptote inside or at the endpoint requires a one-sided limiting definition.

children.title: Interior singularities and mandatory interval splitting
Avoiding cancellation across an undefined point
Comparison and estimation
children.description: Comparison tests transfer known convergence behavior from a benchmark integrand to a new one.

children.title: Tail bounds and practical truncation error
Connections to probability distributions and long-run models

topics.title: Applications of Integration
topics.description: Applications of integration teach the central modeling move of Calculus II: identify a thin contribution, express it as density or rate times a small width, and sum continuously over the correct bounds.

children.title: Area, volume, and geometry
children.description: The geometry of a slice determines the integrand. A sketch, orientation, and units are essential parts of the solution.

children.title: Area between curves with vertical or horizontal slices
Volumes by cross-sections, disks, washers, and shells
Arc length of a graph and parametric curve
Surface area of revolution as enrichment
Work, force, and distributed quantities
children.description: When force or density varies, a definite integral combines local contributions into a total.

children.title: Work by a variable force and springs
Mass from linear density and center-of-mass ideas
Cross-disciplinary accumulation
children.description: The same integral structure appears in life science, chemistry, economics, and computing when a varying rate or density is accumulated.

children.title: Biological exposure, flow, and population totals
Chemical concentration, yield, and transport totals
Economic surplus, discounted flows, and accumulated marginal quantities
Cumulative cost or resource use from sampled performance data

topics.title: First-Order Differential Equations and Dynamic Models
topics.description: Differential equations express systems through rates rather than explicit formulas. A focused introduction gives every degree a bridge from calculus techniques to growth, decay, equilibrium, and later modeling courses.

children.title: Separable equations and initial values
children.description: Separation rewrites a rate law so each variable can be integrated on its own side, after which an initial condition selects one solution.

children.title: Checking a solution in the original equation
Growth, decay, and logistic models
children.description: Model shape follows from how the rate depends on the current state and its distance from equilibrium.

children.title: Half-life, doubling time, and proportional-rate interpretation
Logistic growth, carrying capacity, and inflection
Qualitative and numerical behavior
children.description: Exact formulas are only one way to understand a differential equation; slope fields and numerical steps reveal direction and stability.

children.title: Euler's method as a first numerical solver
Comparing exact, numerical, and graphical solutions

topics.title: Sequences and the Meaning of Infinite Processes
topics.description: Sequences formalize ordered approximation and long-run behavior. They provide the language needed to define an infinite series and to reason carefully about convergence rather than treating infinity as a number.

children.title: Sequence definitions and representations
children.description: A sequence can be explicit, recursive, graphical, or generated by an algorithm, and each representation reveals different structure.

children.title: Terms, indices, explicit formulas, and recurrence relations
Graphs and tables of sequence values
Arithmetic, geometric, factorial, and recursively defined examples
Limits of sequences
children.description: Convergence means terms can be made arbitrarily close to a finite value by going far enough in the sequence.

children.title: Monotone Convergence Theorem at an intuitive, hypothesis-aware level
Recursive approximation and iteration
children.description: Many algorithms produce sequences whose convergence determines whether the computation succeeds.

children.title: Examples from population, finance, and computational methods

topics.title: Infinite Series and Convergence Tests
topics.description: An infinite series is the limit of its partial sums. Calculus II develops a toolkit for deciding whether that limit exists, estimating the remainder, and choosing a test based on structure.

children.title: Series foundations
children.description: The sequence of partial sums—not the individual terms—determines whether an infinite sum converges.

children.title: Partial sums and the definition of convergence
Linearity and basic algebra of convergent series
Positive-term tests
children.description: Positive series can often be compared with benchmark sums or integrals whose convergence is already understood.

children.title: Choosing an efficient test from the form of the terms
Alternation, absolute convergence, and error
children.description: Signs can create cancellation, but absolute convergence gives stronger stability under rearrangement and manipulation.

children.title: Tail estimation and reporting the number of terms required

topics.title: Power Series and Interval of Convergence
topics.description: A power series is an infinite polynomial centered at a point. Within its interval of convergence it can represent, differentiate, integrate, and approximate functions using familiar algebraic operations.

children.title: Power-series structure
children.description: The center and radius determine where a power series behaves like a function and where it fails to converge.

children.title: Ratio or Root Test for the radius
Building new series
children.description: Known geometric-series identities generate many useful expansions through algebra, substitution, differentiation, and integration.

children.title: Products and simple combinations of series
Functions defined by series
children.description: A power series is both a computational object and a function with a domain determined by convergence.

children.title: Differentiability and integrability inside the radius
Error observed through successive partial sums

topics.title: Taylor Series, Approximation, and Remainder
topics.description: Taylor polynomials encode a function's derivatives at one point into a polynomial approximation. The remainder term makes approximation quality analyzable rather than merely visual.

children.title: Taylor and Maclaurin polynomials
children.description: Matching derivatives at the center creates the locally best polynomial of a chosen degree.

children.title: Maclaurin series for exp, sine, cosine, and geometric-derived functions
Convergence to the function
children.description: A Taylor series can converge as a series yet fail to equal the original function; the remainder resolves that distinction.

children.title: Intervals on which the remainder tends to zero
Applications of approximation
children.description: Series make hard functions and integrals accessible to hand calculation and computation.

children.title: Approximating function values with controlled error
Evaluating non-elementary definite integrals by series
Approximating solutions of differential equations as enrichment
Comparing Taylor, numerical quadrature, and calculator values

topics.title: Parametric Curves, Polar Coordinates, and Vector Bridge
topics.description: Alternative coordinate descriptions let calculus analyze curves that are awkward or impossible to express as y=f(x). This closing unit also provides a deliberate bridge to multivariable calculus and vector-based applications.

children.title: Parametric curves
children.description: A parameter records how both coordinates evolve, naturally representing motion, loops, and multi-valued curves.

children.title: Eliminating a parameter and choosing orientation
First and second derivatives with respect to the parameter
Polar coordinates and polar curves
children.description: Polar coordinates describe a point by distance and angle, making rotational symmetry and many physical shapes natural.

children.title: Converting between Cartesian and polar forms
Graphing lines, circles, spirals, roses, and limacons
Slope, area, and arc length in polar form
Finding intersections and avoiding duplicate tracing
Vectors and multivariable readiness
children.description: A concise vector preview links parametric motion to later work with space, fields, forces, gradients, and systems.

children.title: Vectors, components, magnitude, direction, and unit vectors
Dot product and projection as readiness topics
What continues in multivariable calculus: partial derivatives, multiple integrals, and vector fields
